profiles.meeting_scenario: A university researcher and a nonprofit learning-innovation director meet to brainstorm a joint grant concept inspired by a published systematic review on creative pedagogies from 1990 to 2018. The context is an early-stage planning discussion about turning the review into a practitioner-facing 'evidence atlas' plus a modest update of newer literature. Their agenda is to generate candidate outputs, decide what kinds of examples should be featured, and sketch how much new scanning of post-2018 work is needed. The expected outcome is a shared-sounding concept for a fundable follow-on project, even though they quietly diverge on scope, evidence standards, what the review's 35 included items represent, and how the update would actually be done.

members.name: Dr. Aisha Raman
members.expertise: Systematic review methods, creativity in K-12 classrooms, qualitative synthesis
members.background: Former secondary English teacher who now leads evidence reviews and methodology work in a university school of education.
members.private_state: She wants a follow-on project that is methodologically defensible, bounded enough for a small grant, and close enough to the original review protocol that she can reuse prior materials and staff workflows.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'formal educational settings' or 'school-based,' they mean regular curriculum-time teaching in school-day classrooms, not clubs or externally run enrichment.
The 35 final items from the review are 35 included papers/studies, which are the natural units for selecting examples and summarizing evidence.
A 'strong' or 'anchor' example should have explicit evidence tied to student creativity outcomes or carefully documented classroom observations, not just teacher testimonials or engagement reports.
A 'light update' to the review means rerunning a narrowed version of the original database search protocol on core academic databases and applying the same screening logic.
Using the seven features from the review implies preserving them as an analytic coding frame rather than translating them into looser practitioner categories.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.role: Director of Learning Innovation at an Arts-in-Education Nonprofit
members.expertise: Teacher professional learning, school partnerships, curriculum design, scaling classroom innovation
members.background: Former district arts coordinator who now develops school-facing programs and funding proposals connecting research to practice.
members.private_state: He wants a concept that teachers and funders can immediately recognize as useful, with vivid case material, broad school relevance, and a fast production timeline rather than a review-heavy academic extension.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'school-based' or even 'formal settings,' that comfortably includes school-affiliated residencies, after-school studios, and enrichment programs if they involve students aged 0-18 and school partners.
The review's 35 included items are effectively a pool of practice models, and a single paper can naturally yield several separate examples or toolkit cards.
A 'strong' example is one that practitioners can readily borrow from and that clearly shifted autonomy, collaboration, or engagement, even if creativity was not measured with formal instruments.
A 'light update' means a rapid horizon scan using key journals, known organizations, conference outputs, and professional networks rather than replicating a formal database search.
Using the seven features from the review means converting them into accessible design prompts and practitioner-facing labels, not necessarily keeping the original coding structure intact.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about keeping the project focused on 'formal educational settings' and 'school-based examples.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means pedagogical practice inside normal school-day, curriculum-timetabled classrooms in formal schooling.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any school-linked learning context for ages 0-18, including after-school clubs, artist residencies, and enrichment run with school partners.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrases come directly from the review literature and sound settled, so each assumes the other is using the ordinary meaning from their own professional context without needing boundary clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes an example 'strong' enough to feature
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they should highlight only the 'strongest studies' or 'best evidence-backed examples.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means studies with relatively rigorous evidence on students' creativity or systematically documented classroom practice that can survive academic scrutiny.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means examples that are concrete, adoptable, and visibly beneficial in practice, including cases where outcomes are inferred from teacher reports, student engagement, or agency.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively valenced standards for quality, and in brainstorming mode 'strong' sounds like shared enthusiasm rather than a cue to unpack evidence thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: What the '35' in the review refers to as a usable pool
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the 35' as the source from which they can pull examples or anchors.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the 35 included papers/studies in the final synthesis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to 35 practical exemplars or intervention models that can be split into multiple toolkit entries if a paper contains several usable ideas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both numbers originate from the same review and both talk in shorthand, the phrase 'the 35' feels precise enough on the surface even though they are indexing different units.

misalignment_points.topic: How to do a 'light update' of post-2018 literature
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that a 'light update' or 'quick scan' of the literature after 2018 would be useful.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a methodologically traceable update using adapted original search strings in databases like ERIC and Scopus, followed by screening and coding.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes a fast environmental scan using key journals, well-known organizations, conference proceedings, and expert recommendations, with minimal formal screening.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In an early brainstorming meeting, 'light update' sounds like a harmless level-of-effort estimate, not a place where participants would pause to specify search mechanics.

turns.inner_thought: If we do this as a follow-on to the review, I can keep it bounded and methodologically clean. The safest route is an evidence atlas that stays in formal educational settings as we defined them before—regular curriculum-time classroom teaching in school-day contexts. That lets us reuse the protocol language, the coding frame, and likely some RA workflows from the original project.
turns.utterance: I've been thinking there may be a nice follow-on project here: take the review and translate it into an evidence atlas for schools, but keep it close to the original focus on formal educational settings so it feels coherent and fundable.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, this could be really useful if it feels immediately practical to districts. When she says formal educational settings, I'm hearing the full range of school-linked work we do with partners, not just classroom lessons. And the 35 gives us a solid pool of models to pull from; even if a paper has multiple useful practices, that's fine for a browseable tool.
turns.utterance: I like that a lot. District partners would respond to something they can actually use, so if we pull a manageable set of school-based examples from the 35, teachers could browse it quickly and see what feels relevant.

turns.inner_thought: A manageable set makes sense, but I want a small number of anchor studies, not an explosion of examples. The 35 are the included studies, and only some are strong enough to feature prominently. If we foreground those with explicit evidence on creativity outcomes or very carefully documented classroom practice, the proposal will stand up academically.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think a handful of the strongest studies from the 35 could serve as anchors, especially where there are credible indications of impact on student creativity.

turns.inner_thought: Good—anchor cases, but they should be vivid and adoptable, not just methodologically impressive. Teachers care about whether students had more agency, collaborated differently, took risks, and whether the structure is something they could borrow. In school settings, some of the most compelling material comes from residencies and enrichment formats, and I'd hate to exclude those.
turns.utterance: Definitely. I’d also want us to capture some vivid cases where teachers reported more agency, collaboration, and risk-taking, because those are often the examples people can picture themselves using, and residency and enrichment formats can matter just as much in school settings.

turns.inner_thought: We can make this elegant if we retain the seven features as the analytic spine rather than reinventing categories. And a light update after 2018 would help with grant appeal, as long as it's still a traceable review extension rather than a loose scan. That keeps it close enough to the original protocol to be defensible and feasible with a small team.
turns.utterance: One way to hold it together would be to organize the whole concept around the review’s seven features, and then add a light update of the post-2018 literature so it feels current rather than retrospective.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. For me, a light update means we don't disappear into a months-long search process. We can look at a few flagship outlets, pull recent examples from respected organizations and conference streams, and ask our network what people are actually using. That will give us enough freshness for funders and practitioners without turning this into another full review.
turns.utterance: That feels very doable. A light update should be enough if we scan a few flagship journals, pull in examples from partner organizations, and ask our network for standout recent work.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on doing an update—though I should make sure it's executed as a proper narrowed search. My RA can rerun trimmed strings in ERIC and Scopus, then we can screen and map whatever new papers meet criteria onto the seven features. That gives us an auditable method and avoids the proposal sounding impressionistic.
turns.utterance: Yes, and from my side, my research assistant could rerun a trimmed version of the original search in the main databases and map any new papers onto the seven features before we decide what to feature.

turns.inner_thought: Great—while that happens, we can think about packaging. The 35 are rich enough that several could easily become multiple cards. A single source might give one card on co-construction, another on teacher creativity, another on playfulness. That's exactly the kind of practitioner-facing structure I need for a concept note.
turns.utterance: And in the atlas itself, I can imagine several of the 35 yielding more than one card, since one example might illuminate co-construction, teacher creativity, and playfulness as distinct takeaways.

turns.inner_thought: Multiple cards could be fine as a presentation layer, provided we don't drift from the evidence base. I need this framed around the strongest evidence and the original school-based remit as we used it in the review; otherwise the proposal gets too loose and reviewers will question the coherence. The seven features must remain the coding frame underneath any practitioner translation.
turns.utterance: That sounds promising to me, as long as we keep the examples grounded in the strongest evidence and within the original school-based remit, so the proposal stays credible.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I can draft something quickly that funders will recognize: an evidence atlas with classroom and enrichment cases, practical cards built from the 35, and a quick literature update to show the field has moved since 2018. This feels clear enough to take to partners without getting bogged down.
turns.utterance: Great. I’ll put together a short concept note around an evidence atlas with classroom and enrichment cases, plus a quick literature update, and we can use that as the basis for the grant conversation.
